strengths: The distinction between injectivity on discrete token sequences and non-injectivity on continuous embedding spaces is useful. Real-analytic zero-set arguments offer a promising framework for establishing generic injectivity under suitable architectural assumptions.

SIPIT provides a clear, training-free reconstruction procedure using causal structure and access to per-position hidden states. The reported recovery of all 100 tested GPT-2 prompts, with substantial speedup over enumeration, is encouraging.
The manuscript provides extensive mathematical exposition, algorithm pseudocode, and collision-search experiments across several model families.
weaknesses: The headline architectural claim is too broad and admits structural counterexamples. The proof assumes trainable additive positional embeddings (Definitions B.3/B.13), whereas several evaluated models use RoPE. For a RoPE-only causal Transformer without a prepended special token, sequences [a] and [a,a] have identical last-token states in exact arithmetic: all value vectors are identical within each layer, so changing attention weights cannot change their weighted average. This persists through residual connections and positionwise operations for every parameter setting. Consequently, injectivity over all variable-length prompts does not extend to the advertised model class.

The training proof invokes a false mathematical lemma. Lemma C.1 claims that g(ξ₀)=0 makes mixed Hessian blocks of L(g(ξ)h(ξ,ψ)) vanish. Taking scalar g(ξ)=ξ, h(ξ,ψ)=ψ, and L(z)=z gives R=ξψ, whose mixed derivative is 1 at the origin. Lemma C.4 also incorrectly infers independence in a neighborhood from fixing γ=0. Its specific Hessian conclusion might be recoverable using additional properties of the all-zero witness, but the supplied argument does not establish it.

The initialization proof has an additional explicit gap. In Theorem C.2, Case B assigns the same embedding e to both the first mismatching token s_i* and the common final token s_T, while assuming t_i* receives zero. This fails when t_i*=s_T. For example, s=(a,b) and t=(b,b) produce identical embedded inputs under the proposed witness. A revised construction or additional case analysis is needed.

The claimed worst-case linear-time inversion guarantee counts verifier calls rather than computational work. Proposition D.4 establishes at most T|V| tests; each test evaluates a Transformer on a growing prefix, and the gradient policy adds backward passes and vocabulary ranking. Even with KV caching, ordinary dense attention has a cost growing with prefix length. Remark 20 acknowledges per-test costs but does not establish the bounded-cost assumption required by the abstract's linear-time claim.

SIPIT requires the full T×d hidden-state matrix and model parameters, not the single last-token state emphasized by the central theorem. Its correctness only needs token identifiability conditioned on a known prefix. Thus, the experiments do not demonstrate efficient inversion of the paper's principal last-token representation, and several interpretability and privacy conclusions conflate these access settings.

The practical guarantees exceed the assumptions. Absolute continuity over all parameters does not directly cover conventional deterministic bias/normalization initialization or tied parameters, and the training analysis covers GD/SGD rather than common Adam-based training. Real-arithmetic injectivity also supplies no quantitative protection against finite-precision collisions or noise. A positive but unquantified separation margin is insufficient to establish practical losslessness.

The empirical evaluation cannot resolve these issues. Random prompt comparisons and exhaustive next-token continuations do not test structural collisions across lengths or establish universal injectivity. Inversion is evaluated primarily on 100 short GPT-2 Small prompts, without comparable evidence on modern larger models, precision/noise sensitivity, or convincing runtime scaling with sequence length. The adapted HARDPROMPTS baseline and enumeration ablation provide limited evidence for the broader efficiency and novelty claims.

strengths: The distinction between injectivity on discrete token sequences and non-injectivity on continuous embeddings is useful. The analytic zero-set framework provides a promising route to generic injectivity for appropriately specified architectures.

SIPIT offers a simple, training-free recovery procedure using causal structure and token verification. Table 2 reports exact recovery on 100 GPT-2 Small prompts, with substantially lower runtime than vocabulary enumeration.
The collision experiments cover multiple model families, and Appendix D explicitly states the separation-margin condition needed for robust verification.
weaknesses: The training-preservation proof contains a false lemma. Lemma C.1 asserts that a zero multiplicative gate eliminates mixed second derivatives and incorrectly states that a bilinear map has zero second derivative. Taking g(ξ)=ξ, h(ξ,ψ)=ψ, and L(z)=z gives R=ξψ, whose mixed derivative is 1 even at the origin. Lemma C.4 also treats fixing γ=0 as establishing independence from γ in a neighborhood. Its conclusion may be repairable through a direct calculation, but the supplied proof does not establish it.

The architectural scope is substantially overstated. Appendix B assumes learned absolute positional embeddings, which are essential to the separation witness. This does not establish the headline result for RoPE-based models. Indeed, without an imposed BOS token, a standard decoder using RoPE only on queries and keys maps repeated-token sequences such as [a] and [a,a] to identical last-token states: all value vectors are identical, so attention averaging cannot distinguish their lengths. This is a structural collision, not an exceptional parameter choice.

The claimed applicability to standard initialization and training is unsupported. Absolute continuity of the entire parameter vector excludes ordinary deterministic bias and normalization initializations and tied parameters in the stated ambient space. The analysis covers specified GD updates, not common adaptive optimizers such as Adam. These limitations are obscured by repeated claims about practical training pipelines.

The linear-time claim confuses verifier-query complexity with computational complexity. Proposition D.4 establishes at most T|V| tests; each test and gradient update has a prefix-dependent cost. Even cached dense attention generally requires work growing with prefix length. Remark 20 acknowledges per-test costs but does not justify treating them as bounded independently of T.

SIPIT requires the full T-by-d hidden-state matrix and white-box model access, whereas the main theoretical contribution concerns a single last-token state. Its correctness relies only on prefixwise token identifiability. Consequently, the recovery experiments do not operationalize efficient inversion of the headline last-token representation.

The practical evidence is narrow relative to the claims. Exact inversion is principally evaluated on 100 twenty-token GPT-2 Small prompts; broader collision searches do not establish inversion performance on larger models. The comparisons comprise enumeration and an adapted prompt-optimization method, with limited tuning evidence. There are no convincing precision, noise, long-context scaling, or structured-collision stress tests.

Absence of sampled collisions does not establish universal finite-precision losslessness or stable recovery. The positive-margin result supplies no quantitative lower bound, and practical recovery can fail when distinctions fall below numerical precision. The discussion's claims about guaranteed information preservation, probing failures, and privacy therefore exceed the demonstrated results.

strengths: The distinction between non-injectivity on continuous embedding spaces and injectivity on discrete token sequences is useful. The analytic zero-set framework provides a promising approach to formalizing this distinction.

SIPIT offers a simple constructive recovery procedure using causality and candidate verification. On 100 short GPT-2 Small prompts, the reported exact recovery and approximately 139-fold speedup over exhaustive candidate search are encouraging.
The collision experiments cover multiple model families and layers. The appendix also explicitly formulates the separation-margin condition needed for recovery under perturbations.
weaknesses: The training-preservation proof contains a false mathematical lemma. Lemma C.1 claims that g(ξ₀)=0 eliminates mixed Hessian terms, incorrectly asserting that a bilinear multiplication map has zero second derivative. For g(ξ)=ξ, h(ξ,ψ)=ψ, and L(z)=z, the mixed derivative of R=ξψ is 1 even at the origin. Lemma C.4 relies on this lemma and additionally mistakes fixing γ=0 for independence from γ in an open neighborhood. The particular Hessian result may be repairable, but the central training theorem needs a corrected proof.

The architectural scope is substantially overstated. The separating construction uses freely chosen learned absolute positional embeddings, whereas several evaluated models use RoPE. In a RoPE-only causal transformer without an added distinguishing token, prompts consisting of one versus multiple repetitions of the same token have identical last-token states: all value vectors are identical at each layer, so attention cannot distinguish their multiplicity. The paper must restrict its claim or establish appropriate additional assumptions for these architectures.

The initialization and training assumptions do not establish the claimed coverage of practical pipelines. Joint absolute continuity over all parameters excludes ordinary deterministic initialization of biases and normalization parameters, while the analysis covers GD/SGD rather than Adam or AdamW. These limitations are consequential because preservation during standard training is a central contribution.

The headline linear-time guarantee is a verifier-query bound, not a computational runtime bound. Appendix D acknowledges this distinction, but the abstract and main text repeatedly claim linear time. Each verifier or gradient evaluation has a prefix-dependent attention cost; even with KV caching, full attention generally requires work growing with prefix length. Vocabulary ranking adds further overhead.

SIPIT requires every token's hidden state and white-box model access, whereas the main theoretical result emphasizes identification from the last-token state alone. Recovery from the full hidden matrix does not demonstrate efficient inversion of the last-token representation. The practical significance and privacy conclusions should distinguish these observation settings.

The inversion evaluation is narrow: the main comparison uses only GPT-2 Small and 100 prompts of length 20. Larger-model inversion, length-dependent scaling, numerical precision, perturbation robustness, and stronger recovery baselines are missing. Billions of pairwise comparisons among sampled prompts cannot establish universal collision-freedom or a useful worst-case separation margin, especially when many comparisons differ in their final token.

The initialization proof also has an uncovered case in its explicit witness: assigning embedding e to both sᵢ* and the common final token makes the claimed zero embedding for tᵢ* incorrect whenever tᵢ* equals that final token. This appears repairable by changing the construction, but adds to the need for substantial proof revision before acceptance.
